clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive urea cycle disorder caused by deficiency of the mitochondrial ornithine transporter (ORNT1) encoded by SLC25A15
Defined biochemically by the triad of hyperornithinaemia, hyperammonaemia and homocitrullinuria
Presentation is highly variable, ranging from neonatal hyperammonaemic encephalopathy to a chronic course presenting in adulthood
Protein intolerance with self-selected protein aversion and episodic vomiting or confusion is common
Chronic neurological features include spasticity, ataxia, pyramidal signs, seizures and cognitive impairment
Hepatic dysfunction with coagulopathy and raised transaminases can occur and may dominate the picture
The hyperornithinaemia here is distinct from that of gyrate atrophy, which instead causes progressive retinal degeneration
Management is generic: dietary protein restriction, ammonia scavenger therapy and citrulline or arginine supplementation to support the urea cycle
reference.pathophysiology: Ornithine synthesised in the cytosol must be imported into the mitochondrion by the ornithine translocase to combine with carbamoyl phosphate and drive the urea cycle. When SLC25A15 is deficient, ornithine cannot enter the mitochondrion efficiently, so it accumulates in the cytosol (hyperornithinaemia) while intramitochondrial ornithine is insufficient for citrulline synthesis, impairing ureagenesis and causing hyperammonaemia. The excess carbamoyl phosphate is diverted onto lysine to form homocitrulline, producing homocitrullinuria, and is also shunted into orotic acid. Chronic and episodic hyperammonaemia together with the associated metabolic disturbance underlie the neurological and hepatic manifestations.
additionalDifferentials: Ornithine aminotransferase deficiency (gyrate atrophy of the retina)
Ornithine transcarbamylase and other proximal urea cycle disorders
Hereditary spastic paraplegia when the chronic neurological form predominates
additionalInvestigations: Plasma amino acids demonstrating raised ornithine
Plasma ammonia during and between episodes
Liver function tests and coagulation studies
Brain MRI and electroencephalography where neurological features are present
redFlags: Acute hyperammonaemic encephalopathy with vomiting, lethargy or coma
Coagulopathy and hepatic dysfunction indicating liver involvement
Progressive spasticity, ataxia or cognitive decline
Catabolic triggers such as infection, fasting or the postpartum period precipitating crisis
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies with severity and timing of treatment; early diagnosis with protein restriction and citrulline or arginine supplementation can prevent crises and preserve function, whereas late-treated disease may leave fixed neurological deficits.
pitfalls: Confusing the hyperornithinaemia with gyrate atrophy and inappropriately focusing on the retina
Attributing hepatic dysfunction and coagulopathy to primary liver disease rather than the metabolic disorder
Missing the diagnosis in adults with an insidious neurological or psychiatric presentation
Failing to look for homocitrulline, the metabolite that anchors the diagnostic triad
references: Camacho JA et al. Hyperornithinemia-hyperammonemia-homocitrullinuria syndrome and SLC25A15
Summar ML et al. Urea cycle disorders overview
